title: PM says it is 'clear' Russia interfered with Brexit referendum
description: Andy Burnham has said Russia did interfere with the Brexit referendum and warned that similar activities were taking place in France and Germany. The
body: Andy Burnham has said Russia did interfere with the Brexit referendum and warned that similar activities were taking place in France and Germany. The prime minister told The Rest is Politics podcast, external that upon arriving in No 10, he had asked about possible Russian interference in the 2016 vote, adding: "I've had the clear answer that, yes, there was.""I think we've been too much on the back foot on that actually and we haven't informed people sufficiently about the extent to which people are seeking to disrupt the political process from overseas," he added.Burnham did not provide further details about the type or extent of Moscow's activity during the Brexit referendum.Britain Unbound, a pro-Brexit campaign group, said Burnham's comments were "another crude attempt to undermine the legitimacy of the decision that the British people made in 2016". It said that foreign interference in UK elections was "obviously unacceptable" but added: "There is no good reason to believe that Russian intervention influenced the outcome of the referendum in 2016. "It is also insulting to suggest that voters were so easily duped."In his interview, due to be released on Monday, Burnham said he had discussed the problem of Russian interference with Chancellor Friedrich Merz during his visit to Germany earlier this week."There is certainly misinformation, disinformation that is emanating from Russia into German politics," he said.He continued: "These things are important now to put clearly on the record and I believe help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia."It is the first time a UK prime minister has said Russia sought to sway the 2016 Brexit poll but there have long been warnings about efforts by the Kremlin to exert influence on UK politics. In 2020, Parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee published a report into Russian interventions in UK elections and referendums.It did not provide a definitive conclusion on whether Russia had attempted to influence the results of the EU referendum but did criticise successive governments for failing to fully assess or counter the threat.In response, the Russian foreign minister dismissed the report out of hand and called it "Russophobia".And a Kremlin spokesman said Russia did not meddle in other countries' elections.In the same year, however, the then-Conservative government said it was "almost certain that Russian actors sought to interfere" in the 2019 general election.BBC Verify has tracked Russian-linked disinformation campaigns including using AI to create fake videos which impersonate journalists and news organisations reporting on Ukraine. One fake news website falsely claimed that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had bought a mansion owned by King Charles at a discounted price.Earlier this year, Vijay Rangarajan, head of the UK Electoral Commission, told MPs that Russian deepfake videos had been "used extensively in elections around the world"."There is no reason to assume Britain would be an exception," he added. Last month, during his speech to the United Nations, Burnham accused Russian agencies of using "every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people's fears".He announced that the UK would set up a new centre to "stem the poisonous tide" of disinformation. A Downing Street spokesperson said: "We are focused on ensuring our citizens and our institutions are protected from foreign powers and their proxies seeking to threaten lives and undermine our democratic values."We are doing this by strengthening our powers through the National Security Act, strengthening the resilience of our institutions and critical national infrastructure, strengthening our borders, and strengthening our police and intelligence agencies."

schema.headline: PM says it is 'clear' Russia interfered with Brexit referendum

title: Trump says Ukraine and Russia have agreed 'energy ceasefire'
description: Trump's 'energy ceasefire' claim welcomed by Zelensky but Russia silentImage source, Getty ImagesByTinshui YeungUpdated 1 hour agoDonald Trump has cla
body: Trump's 'energy ceasefire' claim welcomed by Zelensky but Russia silentImage source, Getty ImagesByTinshui YeungUpdated 1 hour agoDonald Trump has claimed that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an "energy ceasefire", with Kyiv saying it would support such a move but Moscow yet to comment.The US president insisted that it was "effective immediately" but provided no details.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky initially expressed surprise at the announcement, before saying Kyiv would support it if Moscow did. He also accused Russia of striking Ukrainian energy facilities after Trump's post.Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure - which Kyiv says are vital to curtailing revenue for Moscow's war machine - so Russia can fulfil a recently-struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market.The diesel deal, temporarily undoing sanctions on Russian imports, is attracting growing criticism. Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin. European officials and some US politicians, including from Trump's Republican party, have said they do not support it.The deal is Trump's latest effort to lower domestic fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections, having spent months grappling with the political consequences of the war with Iran which has pushed up global fuel prices, particularly those for diesel.That has soured Trump's standing with the American public, who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation.Figure caption, Watch: What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?Zelensky said it was "news" to him that an energy truce was in effect in comments to news site Axios, before writing on social media that his officials "look forward to clear details of America's dialogue with Russia"."Ukraine is ready not to strike at Russian energy and we count on Russia's similar readiness and on the agreement of the president of the United States of America on this," he said.The BBC has asked the White House for further details.UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now", while France, Canada and the EU also expressed support.Zelensky later said Russia had hit a power plant in Kyiv with a drone, causing power cuts, followed by strikes on energy facilities in the north-eastern Kharkiv region."All of this happened after the president of the United States made his statement about an energy ceasefire," he said.For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure.Moscow said the installations it hits were legitimate targets because they supported Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war".The attacks have disrupted energy supplies on both sides.Image source, Telegram/CrimeanwindImage caption, Huge plumes of smoke seen rising in the skies from the site where the Slavneft-Yanos oil refinery in Russia is located on 6 AugustEarlier on Sunday, UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told the BBC that the UK did not support it, while EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas echoed Zelensky's criticism of it on Saturday.The deal has also attracted criticism from politicians of both main US parties.Seven senators, including three Democrats and four Republicans, have published a statement saying Trump's deal "runs directly counter" to a law that had explicitly banned Russian energy imports."Congress was clear: the US should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our Nato Allies," they said, urging the Trump administration to "reverse course".Republican Senator Thom Tillis, one of the seven, told NBC News that the deal "absolutely will" put American lives at risk.On Saturday Trump accused Zelensky of wanting to "make problems for the world" by continuing to authorise attacks on Russian refineries following the Ukrainian leader's criticism of the diesel deal.The US president suggested that it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president".Zelensky pledged to hold elections - despite them being suspended by the Ukrainian constitution during wartime - if Russia agreed to a 60-day total ceasefire.The Ukrainian president previously resisted calls from the US for fresh elections, pointing to complications with holding a vote in parts of the country that are active war zones or under Russian occupation.Trump, however, has repeatedly accused the Ukrainian leader of using the war to stay in power.Meanwhile, strikes and fighting on the ground continue in the four-year-long war.Six people were killed in attacks on two Ukrainian cities on Sunday, regional officials said.One person was killed in Russia's Belgorod region, which borders Ukraine, while another man was killed in a drone attack in the Russian-occupied Donetsk region, officials said.

schema.headline: Trump says Ukraine and Russia have agreed 'energy ceasefire'

title: Orangutans released back into Borneo forest after devastating fires
description: Eight orangutans have been released back into the wild in Borneo after they were taken into captivity when their habitat was threatened by wildfires o
body: Eight orangutans have been released back into the wild in Borneo after they were taken into captivity when their habitat was threatened by wildfires over the summer.Three mothers, their three daughters and two adult males were freed in a reserve in the west of the island on Friday, International Animal Rescue Indonesia (Yiari) and the forestry ministry said.Indonesian authorities rescued 46 orangutans from fires in August and September. Wildfires in the region are usual for the country's dry season but intensified this year.The apes are critically endangered. Around 104,000 orangutans remain in Borneo and Sumatra, down from more than 230,000 a century ago, according to conservation group WWF.While Indonesia is among many countries to grapple with wildfires each summer, this year's were more intense due to the El Niño ocean warming phenomenon, which makes weather patterns more volatile and intense.Yiari CEO Karmele Llano Sanchez said relocating the eight orangutans to the reserve was a "necessary step" when their habitats became unsafe.Among them was Mama Nopi and her offspring Nopi, Naufal and Nopan, who had been surviving in a coconut and rubber plantation before their rescue in early September, Yiari said.Fires had incinerated the surrounding forestry, restricting their access to food and bringing them closer to humans.

schema.headline: Orangutans released back into Borneo forest after devastating fires

title: Yorkshire Wildlife Park remains closed after fatal tiger attack
description: Yorkshire Wildlife Park remains closed after a man climbed into a tiger enclosure and was fatally attacked by the animal. Emergency services were call
body: Yorkshire Wildlife Park remains closed after a man climbed into a tiger enclosure and was fatally attacked by the animal. Emergency services were called to the park near Doncaster, South Yorkshire, at about 13:30 BST on Saturday after reports of a man climbing down into the enclosure from a walkway. An eyewitness described seeing the man wearing headphones and "pacing around" near the enclosure before he went in and was attacked. Police said the man sadly died at the scene. A park spokesperson said their "thoughts and heartfelt sympathies" remain with the man's family and confirmed the Amur tiger, called Altai, remained in the enclosure and would not be euthanised.The spokesperson says many people had contacted them about the tiger and he was safe and well. Staff who were at the scene who were "deeply affected by events" would receive specialist support, they added.South Yorkshire Police said the man's family were being supported by officers. "Our thoughts are with them at this distressing time," the force said in a statement. It added: "We are aware of videos circulating online and we would encourage people not to share this footage."Earlier on Saturday, in a statement posted on its website, the park said its emergency response procedures had been "immediately activated" and it was "working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened".Ella Ford, 24, from Moreton, Wirral, had visited the park with her boyfriend and filmed the tiger moments before the attack. She described seeing a man by the tiger enclosure "pacing around with his headphones in".A few minutes later, she saw the same man had "climbed up onto the barriers".A woman was close by talking to him, she said, before "he jumped in and crawled in front of the tiger, where the tiger was perched and just lay there".Ford said she then witnessed the tiger grab hold of the man, who she reported as "shouting for help".She estimates around 15 to 20 people were on the enclosure's raised visitor walkway before staff quickly evacuated the area, and shortly afterwards, the park.She described members of the public as being "confused, like what on earth's going on?""I just know some man was obviously trying to bang on the fence to try and deter the tiger away, but it obviously wasn't doing anything," she said.Karmelle Pelham, 39, from Worksop, had been enjoying a family day out when park staff told them the site was being evacuated.She said she had heard what sounded like "gunshots" and an air ambulance had circled above.Pelham added: "There was a big, black tarpaulin over the tiger enclosure." She praised park staff for their handling of the incident, saying it had been "very, very well organised".Foreign Secretary and MP for Doncaster North Ed Miliband said he was "deeply saddened" to hear of the incident and sent his "thoughts and deepest condolences to the family of the individual who died."He added he was "very grateful to the emergency services and staff of the park who responded."Lee Pitcher, MP for Doncaster East and the Isle of Axholme, expressed his gratitude to emergency services for their response.In a statement shared to social media, he said he was "deeply saddened to hear about the tragic incident that has taken place at Yorkshire Wildlife Park today".Yorkshire Wildlife Park opened in 2009, with its Land of the Tigers area opening in 2011.The purpose-built two-acre reserve is home to Amur tigers, an endangered subspecies with around 500 left in the wild.Photos of the enclosure on the park's website shows a high walkway for visitors and fencing above the section where the tigers can roam.Additional reporting by James Kelly

schema.headline: Yorkshire Wildlife Park remains closed after fatal tiger attack

title: Sacha Baron Cohen to star in Quentin Tarantino's West End play
description: Borat actor Sacha Baron Cohen will star in a new play in London's West End from Hollywood director Quentin Tarantino.The Popinjay Cavalier, set in 183
body: Borat actor Sacha Baron Cohen will star in a new play in London's West End from Hollywood director Quentin Tarantino.The Popinjay Cavalier, set in 1830s Europe, was announced earlier this year and is the first play to be written for stage by the US filmmaker, who is also set to direct.Baron Cohen said he was "beyond delighted" to be working with Tarantino, saying: "When the best director in the world calls, you don't ask questions."The director, best known for violent film classics Pulp Fiction and Reservoir Dogs, has said he is "keen with anticipation to give the West End a great night out".The play is set to premiere in March next year, with tickets available from Monday.The production was announced in March this year as a "rambunctious comedy of deception and disguise inspired by the grand swashbuckling epics of stage and screen".Baron Cohen, 54, is known for his self-created comic characters including infamous spoof wannabe gangster Ali G, Kazakh reporter Borat Sagdiyev, and Austrian fashionista Brüno Gehard.He has won two Baftas and three Golden Globes, as well as being nominated for three Oscars and six Emmys.The full cast for The Popinjay Cavalier is planned to be announced at a later date.The play will be co-produced by Sony Pictures Entertainment, which distributed Tarantino's most recent film Once Upon a Time... in Hollywood, and Sonia Friedman Productions, which has overseen hits like Harry Potter and the Cursed Child and Paddington the Musical.The director has repeatedly spoken about planning to retire from movies after making 10 films.He has made nine so far - he counts Kill Bill Volumes One and Two together - and has won two Oscars, for writing Pulp Fiction and Django Unchained.Tarantino revealed his plan to stage a play last summer, telling the Church of Tarantino podcast it was "all written"."It is absolutely the next thing I'm going to do. We'll start the ball rolling on it in January. It's probably going to take up a year and a half to two years of my life, if it's a success and I've got to do the tour version of it and all that," he said."I'm preparing for it to be a success. If it's a flop, I'll be done very quickly."The Popinjay Cavalier will premiere at the Phoenix Theatre on 18 March 2027, with tickets starting from £25.The 63-year-old director lives in Tel Aviv with his Israeli wife, Daniella Pick, and their two children. He told the podcast last year that he would "more than likely move to England and bring my family with me" while working on the play.Tarantino is also known for his forthright personality and made headlines at the end of last year for launching a stinging criticism of actor Paul Dano, as well as in March this year for a spat with Pulp Fiction actress Rosanna Arquette after she criticised the use of the N-word in the 1994 film.

schema.headline: Sacha Baron Cohen to star in Quentin Tarantino's West End play

title: AI is less regulated than milk, Microsoft president says
description: Milk and washing machines are currently more regulated than AI, the president of Microsoft has said.Brad Smith said there needed to be global safety r
body: Milk and washing machines are currently more regulated than AI, the president of Microsoft has said.Brad Smith said there needed to be global safety rules in place, including a legal obligation to tell a "victim" if their system is breached by a rogue AI agent as well as deciding when outside evaluators should sign off on an AI product before it is released.His comments put him at odds with President Donald Trump, who said the sector should regulate itself so US firms don't lose out to Chinese rivals.But Smith said: "Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection."Demands for laws and rules to control AI have grown after experts in the sector said they believed the technology its a threat to humanity.The bosses of the US-based AI giants such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have all backed the idea of an AI development slowdown, but Trump has pushed against this.Speaking to the BBC's Big Boss Interview, Smith called AI both a "tool and a weapon" that urgently needed to be regulated."Let's get started today," he said. He said firms need "emergency brakes" – often known in the industry as 'kill switches' – to pause or slowdown AI if it got out of control in some way. He also said there should be a legal requirement for firms to write "incident reports" and tell victims if the technology goes rogue.  He also suggested that independent government evaluators should vet new AI technology."We know how to do this for other products," Smith said. "We should build on that knowledge and think about how to apply it to AI."Smith said the UK was best placed to drive forward these global rules for AI because of its AI Security Institute, external, launched during former prime minister Rishi Sunak's government as the AI Safety Institute."In the world of technology, in the tech sector, most people that I know would say, if you ask them, name the country that is the leader in having this technical capability, they would say, it's very simple. It's the United Kingdom. They are the best."Smith's views are very different to those of his president, who believes the US should be going full-steam ahead on AI.Trump has repeatedly said that "whoever wins AI, wins".However, Smith does not believe the US government would be as opposed to UK-led AI regulations as Trump's comments make it seem, suggesting the US would be more accepting of the UK making standards than the EU."In Washington DC, people don't look at the UK and they don't look at London the way they look at Brussels – that's a strength," he said."When you look at AI agents that have escaped human control, when you look at models that are so powerful that they're putting the world's cybersecurity at risk. I would say: The moment has arrived. "Let's speak calmly, maybe even softly, but firmly, and start to bring people together. I hope that's the role we can play as a company. I hope that's the role the UK can play as a country."

schema.headline: AI is less regulated than milk, Microsoft president says

title: Poland stabbings driven by online glorification of violence, Tusk says
description: Three violent attacks at Polish schools this week were driven by the "glorification of violence" online, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said.The attacks h
body: Three violent attacks at Polish schools this week were driven by the "glorification of violence" online, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said.The attacks have left one woman dead and others injured, including children."These are very often spontaneous actions inspired by online activity," Tusk said on Sunday, during a crisis meeting with security services. Police have arrested 117 people across the country for possession knives or other weapons, or for threatening to attack schools or fellow students, after searching tens of thousands of schools.A woman was arrested on Saturday after injuring three people while attacking a 17-year-old girl at an educational institution in the capital, Warsaw.It came a day after thousands of police visited schools across Poland, following two stabbing attacks earlier in the week, one of which led to the killing of a female caretaker."We are not dealing with any group organized on a big scale," Tusk said on Sunday. "In the past years and months, we have noted - globally and in Poland - a rise in the fascination with violence," he added.The prime minister said the attacks were acts of "nihilistic violence" associated with the extreme right."Some of the people detained are active in the ultraright environment," he said, adding that police had noticed a rise in online searches of Nazi content as well as of "mass killers who have become idols online".On Wednesday, a 19-year-old student attacked and injured nine people at a vocational school in the central Polish province of Mazovian.A day later, the 37-year-old caretaker was killed after a 15-year-old entered a primary school in Leszczydół-Nowiny, north of Warsaw.Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński also said a 17-year-old was detained in the town of Sierpc, north-west of Warsaw, after allegedly stating "on school grounds that he planned to do something... dangerous - that he intended to harm someone".Thousands of Polish ‌police officers visited schools nationwide to try to reassure pupils after the stabbings sparked rumours of a "Bloody Friday" of more attacks stemming from a supposed online challenge.Meanwhile, Polish security services convened a special meeting on Sunday after receiving information about a potential attack on Tusk and Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, a spokesperson said.A special services spokesman said officials were treating the threat as "deadly serious".

schema.headline: Poland stabbings driven by online glorification of violence, Tusk says

title: Djibouti boat capsize: Children among 139 dead with 84 still missing, UN says
description: At least 139 migrants including 15 children have died and dozens more are still missing after a boat sank off the coast of Djibouti, the UN's migratio
body: At least 139 migrants including 15 children have died and dozens more are still missing after a boat sank off the coast of Djibouti, the UN's migration office has said.The boat had been travelling from Djibouti to Yemen with 305 people aboard when it capsized near the port town of Obock on Thursday night. Around 82 people were rescued, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said.IOM's Djibouti mission chief Alexandre Coissac called the tragedy a "stark reminder" of the dangers migrants face when seeking a new life elsewhere.Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa make the perilous journey each year hoping to reach Gulf countries for safety and work, the agency says.The organisation revised its toll from 109 on Sunday after 30 more bodies were recovered."This is a devastating loss of life," Coissac said. "Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives."Local authorities are also arranging burials for those who have died, while the survivors - all Ethiopian nationals - have medical care readily available to them.Yemen remains engulfed in a devastating civil war that has lasted more than a decade. Despite this conflict - and growing instability across the wider region - migrants still cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen driven by poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change.Since 10 September, the IOM said its Displacement Tracking Matrix had observed more than 20,000 "movements" from Ethiopia to Djibouti.

schema.headline: Djibouti boat capsize: Children among 139 dead with 84 still missing, UN says

title: Man City: Prime Minister Andy Burnham to release details of his meetings with Man City owners
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will release details of his meetings with senior figures at Manchester City following criticism of his comment
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will release details of his meetings with senior figures at Manchester City following criticism of his comments in the wake of the club being found guilty of all charges related to breaches of the Premier League's financial rules.An independent commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than £830m into their football operations.Burnham's previous role as mayor of Greater Manchester has led to questions about his relationship with City's Abu Dhabi ownership, with Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch demanding No 10 release all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club."I've been asked by the leader of the opposition to publish details of my meetings, which I'm happy to do and I'm going to," Burnham told the Rest is Politics podcast. "I will quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as Mayor of Greater Manchester. "None of it is recent, actually, in terms of the meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting, actually, and that was in 2021."The prime minister initially told the BBC he would be "really concerned" if Manchester City's owners decide to sell up following the guilty verdict before later denying his reaction had "downplayed the seriousness of the findings".However, some Premier League clubs were so "astonished" by Burnham's stance that sources told BBC Sport they were "concerned" about political interference in the appeal process. Sanctions are yet to be announced and City have lodged an appeal against the verdict.City returned to action for the first time since the guilty verdict when they played at Liverpool on Sunday, winning 3-0.Burnham was mayor of Manchester from 2017 until earlier this year and his tenure took place during a sustained period of success for City.As mayor, he championed investment from the Gulf as a way of growing Manchester's economy, a strategy which was initially pursued by the city's leaders before Burnham became the inaugural elected mayor of the Greater Manchester Combined Authority."I don't think I misspoke," said Burnham of his past comments on Man City's owners. "What I would say is my mind hadn't been on all of the issues. My mind had been on Labour Party conference and I was doing interviews in relation to it."And also, I didn't link those two things. You know, the questions linked those two things. What I would say is they're very separate."The football issues are different from the investment issues. People will try and conflate those two things, but they shouldn't, in my view. "The football issues, the findings of the independent commission are serious, as I said in the interview."The entire process involving the charges against Manchester City is independent of the Premier League.An independent commission held a 42-day hearing in 2024 which led to the verdict announced last month, with City also guilty of all charges except one relating to non-cooperation with the Premier League investigation.The commission's report said that "a number of important club witnesses gave false evidence in key respects and that some knowingly gave untrue and dishonest evidence".A separate independent appeal board will hear City's appeal. The club continues to deny any wrongdoing.

schema.headline: Man City: Prime Minister Andy Burnham to release details of his meetings with Man City owners

title: Australia v South Africa: Pace attack and Steve Smith put tourists in charge
description: Australia veterans shine against South AfricaImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Steve Smith now has 223 catches in Test cricket, three more than
body: Australia veterans shine against South AfricaImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Steve Smith now has 223 catches in Test cricket, three more than Joe Root in second place for non-wicketkeepersByMatthew HenryBBC Sport JournalistUpdated 4 hours agoFirst Test, Durban (day three of five)Australia 390 & 33-0: Maddinson 17*South Africa 284: Bedingham 49; Cummins 3-54Australia lead by 139 runsScorecardAustralia's modern Test side remain a fascinating one to unpick.Viewed by many in England as there for the taking in last winter's Ashes despite a 4-1 win, they are also labelled too old by many observers at home.The victims of recent shock defeats by West Indies and Bangladesh, they are still unbeaten in their past nine Test series.But while their struggling batting line-up was bailed out by Matt Renshaw across the first two days of the first Test in Durban, they took control over South Africa on day three in an all-too familiar way.Nine years after they first appeared together as Australia's bowling quartet, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood, Pat Cummins and Nathan Lyon produced their latest relentless performance to dismiss South Africa for 284. There was even some magic from Steve Smith thrown in too.Cummins took three wickets, Starc, Hazlewood and Lyon two apiece, in doing so brushing off any doubts about their effectiveness at the start of a run of Tests against the world Test champions, in-form New Zealand, India and England.How Australia's quartet turned the screw on South AfricaAt 82-1 in response to Australia's 390, South Africa appeared well in the Test on a relatively good surface.Australia's bowlers searched for early swing and Aiden Markram and David Bedingham countered with a second-wicket partnership which progressed at almost 4.5 runs per over.It was then, at the 20-over mark, captain Cummins reverted to Australia's tried and tested - Lyon one end, the quicks rotating at the other.Having bowled 34% of their deliveries full in the first 20 overs, Starc, Hazlewood and Cummins dragged back their lengths. There were only 19 deliveries pitched fuller than six metres between the 20th and 60th overs.With deliveries easy to hit scarce, Markram and Bedingham attempted forced back-foot drives and edged to slip for 37 and 49 respectively.Image source, CricVizImage caption, South Africa were 82-1 after 20 overs (left graphic) but were 214-8 after Australia dragged their lengths back between the 21st and 60th overs (right graphic)Wiaan Mulder was caught in two minds and bounced out by Cummins. Tristan Stubbs top-edged the Australia captain to fine leg.In Australia's first innings, Renshaw, who ground out a superb 190, faced 52 deliveries pitched as short and played a pull or hook shot to four of them. He scored runs with only one of those shots - when he had 176 runs to his name and had faced 368 balls.The contrast to Renshaw's application could not have been greater.Six overs after Stubbs was caught, Marco Jansen, who had struck six fours in quickly reaching 26, also tried to pull Hazlewood off a fuller length and was tamely caught at mid-off.The quality of the bowling and fact the Proteas are playing their first Test since November were other factors in South Africa's slide.Smith soars back to number oneAt the other end, off-spinner Lyon bowled 19 overs at less than three runs per over.The 39-year-old had a more worn pitch to utilise than South Africa's spinners and found significantly more turn and threat.He also had the sprawling Steve Smith to his advantage.Both of Smith's catches off Lyon, first to dismiss Temba Bavuma and then Kyle Verreynne, were feats of anticipation. He saw both right-handers shape to reverse sweep, gambled and clung on at close range. The first was good. The one-handed second was spectacular."He's an absolute freak," said Lyon. "He practices that in training."He is an incredible thinker of the game but the way he moves, premeditates, for those types of catches."There are not many people in the dressing room that would be able to pull off those two catches."In between, Smith's leaping catch at second slip after Cummins found Bedingham's edge took the 37-year-old back above Joe Root as the non-wicketkeeper with the most catches in Test history on 223.While he ended the day with three more catches than Root, he still has a catch percentage about 77%, which sits below the format average.He creates, and occasionally drops, chances such as these - chances others would not have created.Pace cartel appears as good as everThe result is Australia's fabled foursome now have 607 wickets in Tests in which they have played as a quartet.The next most successful bowling four-pronged attack is James Anderson, Stuart Broad, Ben Stokes and Moeen Ali, who took 415 wickets in their 31 Tests together for England."Each of these players will go down as a legend of Australian cricket," said former Australia bowler Jason Gillespie on ABC Radio."Starc got hit for a few early but I didn't mind that. "Hazlewood was very good, as he always is. Cummins was hostile. He looked fresh."Much has been made of Australia's ageing side and a perceived lack of succession planning.At 37, Starc is the oldest of the three quicks but his average pace of 141.21km/h in 2026 is higher than any of his past three years. He is also averaging his most swing in a calendar year since 2015.The concern for Australia comes when they are not fit, with Hazlewood having missed all five of last winter's Ashes Tests and Cummins four.Australia's issue right now is keeping each of their quartet on the field, because they appear as good as ever.At 33-0, Australia lead South Africa by 139 runs.Even with bad light halting play early again, they should have the time to press home an advantage across the Test's final two days.

schema.headline: Australia v South Africa: Pace attack and Steve Smith put tourists in charge

title: Pope Leo XIV to have surgery after nodule found on lung
description: Pope Leo XIV has announced he will be operated on "in the coming days" after a nodule was found on his lung during a medical check-up."The doctors fou
body: Pope Leo XIV has announced he will be operated on "in the coming days" after a nodule was found on his lung during a medical check-up."The doctors found an early, well-localised nodule on my lung," he told the public during his weekly Sunday prayers in St Peter's Square in Rome.The 71-year-old said his medical team "believe it would be right to intervene" and he had agreed to the operation, while reassuring pilgrims that the mass was "well-contained" and caught "at an early stage".The pontiff's admission that he would need surgery comes nearly a year-and-a-half after he succeeded the late Pope Francis, who also experienced issues with his lungs that required hospital treatment.Leo concluded his Angelus prayer by thanking everyone for their "spiritual closeness" and said he entrusted himself to their prayers.Holy See Press Office spokesman Matteo Bruni told the media that "the operation is scheduled for the first days of next week".He added that the Pope is expected to take about a week to recover.Vatican News, the Holy See's news portal, said the operation will take place at Gemelli Hospital in Rome.The hospital set up a special Papal suite following the failed assassination attempt on Pope John Paul II's life in May 1981, which is still in use today.Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed her "personal solidarity" with the Pope as he "faces the ordeal ahead in the coming days".Her sentiments were echoed by Italian President Sergio Mattarella, who offered his "sincerest wishes for a peaceful recovery and a speedy and full return to health".Isaac Herzog, the president of Israel, also wished the pontiff "a full and speedy recovery".The Pope, born Robert Francis Prevost, is the 267th occupant of the throne of St Peter – the first US citizen to do so.He was ordained in 1982 and spent years as a missionary in Peru, where he is remembered as a figure who worked with marginalised communities.During Sunday's service, the Pope confirmed his upcoming visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in November will still go ahead.The Archbishop of Montevideo, Daniel Sturla, said preparations for his tour will continue with "greater enthusiasm" as he called for prayers for his recovery.A lung nodule is a small lump of tissue that is usually detected following an X-ray or CT scan of the chest, according to the NHS.Most nodules do not cause other symptoms.

schema.headline: Pope Leo XIV to have surgery after nodule found on lung

title: Iran war threatens Healey's Budget plans, think tank warns
description: The price spike caused by the US-Israel war in Iran poses a major challenge for Chancellor John Healey as he puts together his first Budget, an influe
body: The price spike caused by the US-Israel war in Iran poses a major challenge for Chancellor John Healey as he puts together his first Budget, an influential think tank has warned.Higher-than-expected inflation could eat into what the government hoped to spend on public services, meaning Healey will have to choose between spending cuts, tax rises, or a mixture of both, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said.It urged the government to ensure its spending plans are credible, as opposed to proposing unrealistic future cuts to make the Budget add up. The Treasury declined to comment on "rumour and speculation". However, speaking ahead of the annual International Monetary Fund meeting this week, Healey said: "The consequences of conflict in the Middle East and Europe are hitting countries worldwide, leading to higher prices at the pumps and more expensive mortgages at home."But Britain and our allies can face up to these challenges together."He said his Budget "will build on this approach with fiscal discipline helping to deliver economic resilience" and give people "breathing space".However, the government is under growing pressure to show financial markets that it has a tight grip on finances as the cost of borrowing rises.The IFS cautioned Healey about making any spending announcements in the 28 October Budget speech he has no intention of honouring."A 'steady-as-she-goes' Budget is not an option available to the chancellor," said IFS director Helen Miller said."Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments' spending plans off course."Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the Budget a work of fiction," she added.The US-Israel war against Iran and Russia's invasion of Ukraine have together helped drive up energy prices around the world.These higher costs have been passed to customers via higher prices on shelves and at the pumps. The wars have also contributed to a rise in the cost of UK government debt interest payments, adding to the pressure on Healey.Although higher inflation will boost tax revenues, it will also eat into the value of departments' cash budgets, the IFS said.Like other analysts, the IFS thinks recent turbulence on bond markets and higher inflation will add around £10bn to forecasts for the government's borrowing costs in 2029-30.However, it still expects the government to meet its self-imposed fiscal rules - that it will only borrow for investment projects by the financial year 2029-30 and also be reducing debt as a percentage of GDP - not least as inflation pushes up tax revenues.But it expects those rules to be met by a smaller buffer - known as "headroom" - of around £20bn. That is less than the £24bn buffer predicted at the time of the Spring Statement by the official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR). Recent indications have been that the markets would be comfortable with that degree of reduced headroom. The IFS also expects any "breathing space" help for households to be temporary and limited in scale.However, the IFS warns that in such a volatile environment, its forecasts are exceptionally uncertain. And the official forecast from the OBR - which the chancellor relies on when making his plans - may come to a very different conclusion.The IFS reckons that to maintain departments' budgets in the face of higher inflation, the government may need to find an extra £25bn in 2029-30.That is before consider considering the ambition to raise defence spending. Raising such an amount would point to significant tax rises.The chancellor does not have to address spending totals in this Budget, and may choose to leave such decisions until future events - for example, next year's Spring Statement or Spending Review - by which time the outlook for the economy could look very different.But the IFS warned that the spending plans inherited from the previous chancellor, Rachel Reeves, would mean some departments' budgets would not keep pace with inflation in a few years time.It said not addressing this would cast doubt on the credibility of the government's plans.However, previous chancellors have relied on a similar strategy of pencilling in unrealistic future spending plans to ensure that they meet the fiscal rules on the day - only to change the plans further down the line.

schema.headline: Iran war threatens Healey's Budget plans, think tank warns

title: Singapore Grand Prix: Lewis Hamilton apologises to Ferrari as Kimi Antonelli moves to brink of title
description: Lewis Hamilton apologised to his Ferrari team after overriding the pit wall and choosing his own strategy during the Singapore Grand Prix.Ferrari were
body: Lewis Hamilton apologised to his Ferrari team after overriding the pit wall and choosing his own strategy during the Singapore Grand Prix.Ferrari were on course to finish second and third with Charles Leclerc and Hamilton, but instead the seven-time champion fell back to sixth in the closing laps as he fought a losing battle to hold off three cars while on fading tyres.Hamilton apologised to the team over the radio on the slowing-down lap after the race, saying: "Sorry, boys. I let you down today with that strategy. My call, and I lost us valuable points. I'll try and make up for it in the next one."Team principal Frederic Vasseur said: "Clearly we asked them to pit. Charles pitted. Lewis didn't want to pit because he... I don't know why. And then he realised it was the wrong call. It's why he apologised to the team."Now it's not a drama for me that he made the wrong call. I'm making mistakes, he's making mistakes, we're all making mistakes sometimes. Now we have to look ahead and make mistakes positively."Hamilton did not speak to the media after the race after saying he felt unwell and being given permission to miss the interview zone, known as the media pen.In a statement released by Ferrari, he said: "Under the virtual safety car, the team called me in but I missed the entry.  After that, I decided to stay out and try to hold track position to the end but in the closing laps, I was struggling massively with tyre degradation and lost three places, finishing P6, which doesn't reflect the pace we had in the car."A painful lesson, but I take full responsibility for the decisions I made. Not every call will work out, and I can accept getting it wrong but I'm sorry for the team for the points we lost today. They put so much into every weekend, and I wanted to deliver more for them. I'll continue to put the work in and come back fighting at the next race."Ferrari called both cars in to the pits during a virtual safety car that was called mid-race. Stopping under the VSC saves about 10 seconds versus stopping under racing conditions.Hamilton said in the statement that his decision was based on his improved pace on the soft-compound tyre after he had been forced to make an earlier pit stop than planned because the medium tyre on which he started the race was not performing."At a track [where it's] difficult to overtake, you need to try something different and I chose to start on a new medium tyre, to go long and try to make a one-stop work," he said."Unfortunately the medium didn't perform as well as the soft. I had a good second stint and the pace was back, but I couldn't make the progress I needed."His first stop was six laps before Leclerc's and when the Monegasque emerged on to the track, Hamilton was right behind him and initially faster.At one stage, he pointed out to the team that he had "lost two seconds on that lap", but the team decided not to invert the cars. Hamilton followed Leclerc within two seconds for a further 10 laps before slowly starting to lose ground a couple of laps before the VSC.Vasseur said the team decided to leave Leclerc in front because he had pitted later than Hamilton."The tyre advantage was for Charles, that he pitted six laps later," Vasseur said. "I think it was the right call."However, that argument appears to be somewhat undermined by the fact that the medium tyre emerged as the worst option for the race - as Hamilton had found out in the first stint and other drivers later discovered.Leclerc was put back on the soft when he stopped under the VSC.Hamilton's error means Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli is in a position to clinch his first world title at the next race, the US Grand Prix in Austin, after finishing third behind race winner Max Verstappen and Leclerc.Antonelli's lead over team-mate George Russell, who finished ninth after starting from the back of the grid, has extended to 102 points and 111 over Hamilton.The Italian needs to leave Austin with an advantage of at least 125 points to clinch the title, with five races at most remaining after that.He will do so if he wins the race with Russell finishing ninth or lower and Hamilton fifth or lower at the Circuit of the Americas on 25 October.If he becomes champion this year, the 20-year-old will be the youngest in Formula 1 history.Asked if he would be daring to dream about the title on the flight home, he said: "For sure, but at the same time, I know it's very close, I know it's there, but I just need to make sure that I keep doing the best I can."The mindset is always the same, to go out there and win and perform the best way I can."This weekend I haven't particularly driven that well. I felt like I could have done a better job, but I feel confident that a week to reset and I'm really looking forward to being back in Austin."But at the end of the day, if I don't do my job well, then the result won't come. So in order to achieve what I want, I need to perform, as simple as that."There is some doubt about the mathematics of the championship because it is not completely clear how many races are remaining.F1 is pushing ahead with the original schedule, which ends with two races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, despite the war in the Middle East, having been reassured the countries are safe.But if the war intensifies before mid-November, those races will have to be cancelled. In that event, the season would end at Imola in Italy, on the same 6 December date as Abu Dhabi, after a two-week break following the Las Vegas race on 22 November.Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff said: "I haven't looked at it from that perspective, because the moment I have the thought of 'how many points is it actually, and when could he win it,' I remind myself that this is motor racing and crazy things have happened."The aim must be to score points, not to lose too many on the others, like today, gaining on Lewis, which was unexpected, and then it's going to come towards him, whether that's in Mexico or Brazil [immediately after Austin] or further down the line."Mercedes split their cars between two different specifications in Singapore in an attempt to understand why a major upgrade introduced at the previous race in Malaysia did not work.Antonelli drove the new spec and Russell the old, and by the end of the weekend the team said they had made some progress in understanding the new aerodynamic package.Antonelli said: "We're just trying to understand how to extract more potential out of it because we do see the gains, we do see what it could bring."It's just that the window is very small at the moment where the car operates and is very sensitive to the way you drive it, the way you take a corner, the way you brake. So it reacts very differently."So hopefully now in Austin, we have three free practices, so we can be very open-minded with set-up and hopefully we can find a way and we can use the full potential of the package and finally see the gains."Russell was asked how he viewed the rest of the season now the championship was almost over. He replied: "The goal is to improve the car. We were dominant for so long and since the break we have seen Red Bull be exceptionally fast on many different types of circuits and we need to go back to winning ways."Verstappen's victory was his first grand prix win in Singapore. It was also his second in succession, emphasising Red Bull's return to the front after a difficult start to the season."Very different tracks that we have gone well at now. That's of course always nice to see," said the 29-year-old."Our car has taken a really nice step forward. It's just been more driveable and more predictable. That's what I wanted and needed from the car to find that last step to fight up front. And I hope that we can carry that momentum forward."We don't really have anything to win in the championship, right? Kimi is miles ahead. I don't care if I'm second, third or fourth. It doesn't do anything. But I just want to have fun until the end, you know, try to go for a day's success."But the four-time champion was cautious about the prospect of being competitive at every race before the end of the season."It's very difficult to say and I don't want to say now that I will be in the fight in Austin," he said."Yeah, the last few weekends have been great. But I just take it race by race and once we are in Austin, then we'll see how it will go there. But it's again a very different track."From what I saw in WEC (the World Endurance Championship), the track is incredibly bumpy. Oh my God, yeah, I'll probably need to order a new spine, I think, after the weekend. Yeah, I'll become like Robocop. Yeah, crazy. That's again a new challenge for everyone, to deal with those bumps."And then we just go from there. We have to go to Mexico, high altitude, everything will run super hot, and we need to see how the engine is going to perform in that altitude, how the car is behaving, because it's very different."So there are so many different things that you can get right or wrong in those races."

schema.headline: Singapore Grand Prix: Lewis Hamilton apologises to Ferrari as Kimi Antonelli moves to brink of title

title: Drumcree: It's within DUP's gift to remove O'Neill as first minister, says Lockhart
description: The DUP (Democratic Unionist Party) share power with Sinn Féin in the Northern Ireland Executive, but Lockhart says it can no longer be business as us
body: The DUP (Democratic Unionist Party) share power with Sinn Féin in the Northern Ireland Executive, but Lockhart says it can no longer be business as usual."You can not continue to engage with someone who is so blatant in her disregard and disdain for a large section of this community," she said. "Very clearly it cannot be business as usual at Stormont."Lockhart says her party must take action against O'Neill. "People want to see consequences, and we have said very clearly, profound consequence, and therefore we should use whatever is in our armoury to ensure that Michelle O'Neill, the person who really is supposed to be that first minister for all, as she claims, is dealt with in the appropriate way," she added.The DUP could remove O'Neill from the first minister's position if the deputy first minister quits. That role is held by Emma Little-Pengelly, but that seems unlikely.Sinn Féin assembly member John O'Dowd rejected claims that the move to ban the parade went in favour of his party, saying "the decision went in the way of the residents" who he said have "faced an awful four weeks" since the application to walk was lodged.O'Dowd, who is also finance minister in the executive, was one of a number of Sinn Féin politicians who joined a protest with residents on the Garvaghy Road.On Thursday, the police said they had begun issuing letters inviting people "reasonably suspected" of committing offences linked to the protests to interview.Speaking on BBC News NI's Sunday Politics programme, O'Dowd said: "I own my decision", adding that he thinks it was "the right thing to do"."I got into politics to stand against the intimidation of communities such as the Garvaghy Road, who went through hell and high water over many, many years."I stood with the people of the Garvaghy Road. I will continue to stand with the people of Garvaghy Road because it was the right thing to do."He added that he believes the community responded in "a peaceful, democratic way" to the decision to approve a march on 27 September."I would appeal, not only to Gavin, but maybe hopelessly to Carla and others, to calm their language and to show responsible leadership and calm leadership at this stage," he added."I don't think that continued demonisation or an attempt to criminalise the community of the Garvaghy Road is an appropriate way forward."What we need in Portadown is reconciliation."

schema.headline: Drumcree: It's within DUP's gift to remove O'Neill as first minister, says Lockhart

title: Saudi Arabia's Riyadh airport hit by second Houthi strike in two days
description: One person has been killed and 11 injured in a second strike on the international airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, officials have said.A Saudi mil
body: One person has been killed and 11 injured in a second strike on the international airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, officials have said.A Saudi military spokesman said a projectile had hit King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, causing a fire in one of its passenger halls. Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said in a statement on X that one person, a Pakistani resident, had been killed in the attack.It comes a day after a strike on the same airport killed 13 people and injured 308 others, following similar strikes earlier this week.The Houthis in Yemen said they were behind the attacks and warned airlines and passengers against using Saudi Arabian airports and airspace.The group said they had targeted the airport with a mix of ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as drones in the past 24 hours.They also attacked oil facilities and Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, their military spokesman Brig Gen Yahya Saree said.He vowed to continue the "escalating operations deep inside Saudi Arabia", warning that all Saudi airports were potential targets apart from those in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.The Houthis have said they are targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war, as well as an air strike on the airport in Sanaa.On Sunday Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition, said air defences had intercepted a missile near the airport in Riyadh, while authorities were dealing with the fire caused by an "unknown projectile" that hit Passenger Hall No 4.US President Donald Trump has said the US would "make a decision" and "move very quickly" on whether to strike the Houthis, while UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting suggested the UK could "potentially" provide more support for Saudi Arabia.Saturday's strike was the deadliest single attack on a Gulf Arab country since the war between Israel, the US and Iran began in February. The Saudi-led coalition vowed to respond, calling it a "war crime".Four Saudi nationals, two people from Bangladesh and one person each from the US, Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt were among the dead, the Saudi civil aviation authority said. The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said on Sunday that an Indian man had succumbed to the injuries he sustained in the attack.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attacks and confirmed that a US citizen was killed in the strikes. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said he was "appalled".The UK Foreign Office is advising against all travel to parts of Saudi Arabia, including areas within 10km (6.2 miles) of the border with Yemen, while other western embassies have warned their nationals about travel in the region.

schema.headline: Saudi Arabia's Riyadh airport hit by second Houthi strike in two days
